79.0.s.en: (1) The destruction of Jerusalem and the temple

79.0.0.en: 1- O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps. The psalm prophesies about the entry of the pagans into Jerusalem, God's inheritance, since they are His only people who worship Him in the Old Testament; and they defiled His temple by entering it, and burned it, and made it and Jerusalem a ruin like heaps of stones and dust. And although this was a dreadful thing in the eyes of the Jews, since they thought that the temple would remain firm until the end of the world, they were shocked by its destruction, and forgot that they had broken God's commandments and worshiped idols, so the natural result was that God departed from them and let His temple be ruined, which they had already ruined by their deeds.

79.1.0.en: 2- The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth.

79.1.1.en: 3- Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them.

79.1.2.en: The psalm describes the multitude of the slain in Jerusalem at its destruction, showing that the corpses were cast down everywhere, and blood flowed from them, and the Jews could not bury the corpses because of their great number, so the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth ate them. All this was because they rejected God's commandments, so God rejected them. And the enemies were hard of heart, so they killed the Jews and cast their corpses inside Jerusalem, and likewise they shed the blood of everyone who tried to flee, around Jerusalem.

79.2.0.en: 4- We are become a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and derision to them that are round about us.

79.2.1.en: By the destruction of Jerusalem it became a disgrace and a mockery in the eyes of its neighbors, such as the Edomites who gloated over it and seized the Jews who were fleeing and handed them over to their enemies (Ps 137:7), noting that the neighbors of the Jews had been enslaved to them in the days of David and Solomon, so they seized this opportunity to gloat over them.

79.2.2.en: When any affliction comes upon you, examine yourself lest your sins be the cause, and return to God with repentance, and trust that He is able to heal you, build you up, and compensate you for all that you have missed.

79.3.s.en: (2) Turning G's anger away from His people

79.3.0.en: 5- How long, LORD? wilt thou be angry to the uttermost? shall thy jealousy burn like fire?

79.3.1.en: The psalmist pleads with God to stop His anger and His jealousy toward His people. The anger meant is the discipline of the people, that they may repent. As for jealousy, it is God's love for His people, who does not want them to turn aside from Him to the worship of idols and evil; for God has no passions like human beings. And this verse shows the extent of the suffering of God's people, and at the same time their hope in God who rescues them and lifts His disciplines from them.

79.4.0.en: 6- Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen that have not known thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name.

79.4.1.en: 7- For they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling place.

79.4.2.en: Pour out: to pour abundantly; it is from the verb "to overflow".

79.4.3.en: The psalmist also asks God not only to cease from disciplining His people, but to turn His anger upon the Gentiles, for two reasons:

79.4.4.en: 1- That the Gentiles do not know God and do not worship Him.

79.4.5.en: 2- That they wronged God's people violently and destroyed them, as he says "devoured". So he cries to God to save His people, to drive the enemies away from them, and to take vengeance on them, that they may know the corruption of their evil, perhaps they will return to God.

79.4.6.en: Do not be troubled by God's disciplines of you, for they are temporary and are for your good. And do not doubt when those who wrong you gain power, because God hates their evils and will punish them. Do not gloat over them, nor be filled with rage against them, but correct their faults with repentance, and pray for those who wrong you that they may return to God.

79.5.s.en: (3) The salvation of G and thanksgiving to Him

79.5.0.en: 8- O remember not against us former iniquities: let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low. The psalmist comes to God with humility and lowliness, and asks Him for two things:

79.5.1.en: 1- That He not remember the sins of their fathers, for they are many, and He has promised that every person bears his own guilt, so the children are not punished for the sin of the fathers (Ezek 18:2-4).

79.5.2.en: 2- He asks for God's forgiveness and mercies for the present sins of the people.

79.5.3.en: And in this God quickly lifts His anger from His people; because they are in severe affliction and were almost perishing.

79.6.0.en: 9- Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and forgive our sins, for thy name's sake.

79.6.1.en: 1- The psalmist asks three blessings of God, which are:

79.6.2.en: a- His divine help to bear the sufferings.

79.6.3.en: b- That He deliver them from the hands of their enemies.

79.6.4.en: c- That He forgive them their sins that caused them these disciplines.

79.6.5.en: 2- The people do not deserve these blessings, but the people ask for them for the sake of God's name. And what is meant by the name of God the Savior is Christ, incarnate in the fullness of time. This verse shows the humility of the people and their confidence that salvation is from the hand of God alone, and that every blessing they need is a divine gift.

79.7.0.en: 10- Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God? let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed.

79.7.1.en: Shed: poured out, that is, that which flows on the ground.

79.7.2.en: The writer asks God not to leave the pagan Gentiles believing in their strength and their gods and despising You, the great God, when they say, Where is our God? Why did He not rescue us from their hands? Therefore we ask that You avenge the blood of Your people that has flowed on the ground, so that they may know that You alone are the great God, and that their gods are nothing, perhaps they will believe and return to You.

79.8.0.en: 11- Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee; according to the greatness of thy power preserve thou the sons of death;

79.8.1.en: 1- In humility again the writer asks God to accept the prayers of the captives, who are the Jews taken captive by Assyria and Babylon, because they are in humiliation, indeed counted among the dead, since they have no freedom or ability to move and return to their land to worship God. And he asks also that He preserve His children, who from the severity of the enemies' pressure and humiliation of them have become as good as dead.

79.8.2.en: 2- The arm of God is a symbol of the Incarnation of Christ, for He is the Word of God and His power, which is very great, so he asks God to hasten to save His people who are dead, not only because they are in the humiliation of the bondage of captivity, but also because they will go down to Hades, but by the Incarnation of Christ He saves them and moves them from Hades to Paradise.

79.9.0.en: 12- And render unto our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, wherewith they have reproached thee, O Lord.

79.9.1.en: 1- The psalmist asks God to show His justice, and take vengeance on the wicked enemies of His people according to their cruelty to His people, punishing them sevenfold for what they did, so that they may know the hideousness of evil and turn back from it, and know the power of God who is above all gods, and so disgrace and shame come upon the enemies.

79.9.2.en: 2- Perhaps what is meant by the enemies of God's people is the demons who try to draw God's people away from faith and the worship of God, so he asks for vengeance on them sevenfold, that is, in eternal torment.

79.10.0.en: 13- So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever: to generation after generation we will shew forth thy praise. The psalm ends with a great hope that the writer saw by faith, which is that God will rescue His people and bring them back to their land, and they will build the temple and worship Him, and then their voices will rise in thanksgiving and praise to God for the greatness of His works. And this praise continues from generation to generation, that is, forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

79.10.1.en: How great are God's works with you, for He is ever caring and watching over you; therefore He deserves from you constant thanksgiving and praise. And this thanksgiving and praise fills your heart with joy; for He bestows on you His fellowship, so you pass through afflictions without weariness, because you feel His presence with you.

79.10.2.en: The right hand of God restores us and shepherds us. To the chief Musician upon the Lily. A testimony. Of Asaph. A psalm. "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel) "... v. 1) Introduction:

79.10.3.en: 1- Its writer: Asaph, the head of the singers in the days of David.

79.10.4.en: 2- Why was it written? It is a prophecy about the Jews taken captive in the Babylonian captivity, who ask God to bring them back from the captivity, and to care for His people and His temple that the enemies burned.

79.10.5.en: 3- This psalm is said to the accompaniment of a musical instrument called the lily, as appears in the title of the psalm. It is an instrument resembling the lily flower.

79.10.6.en: 4- The title of the psalm declares that it is a testimony; that is, it bears witness to the faith of God's captive people, their suffering, their prayers, and their hope of returning from captivity.

79.10.7.en: 5- The title declares that it is a psalm; that is, it is sung to the accompaniment of the pipe.

79.10.8.en: 6- This psalm speaks about the Church, or the suffering human soul, which believes in God and so prays and pleads to Him to lift its sufferings from it and to take care of it with His care.

79.10.9.en: 7- This psalm longs for God to become incarnate and redeem mankind, and to take care of His children who believe in Him, and shepherd them forever.

79.10.10.en: 8- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.

80.0.0.en: 1- Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like sheep; thou that sittest upon the cherubims, shine forth.

80.0.1.en: 1- The psalmist pleads with God, and describes Him as the Shepherd of Israel, that is, God's people before the division. And he reminds Him that He is the leader of Joseph, who bore many troubles from his brothers and remained steadfast in his chastity. And he is poor like the sheep, that is, the weak lamb before wolves. So he needs Your care and Your leading, O God, especially since You are the great God, able to do all things, who sits upon the cherubim who are full of eyes, and praise You continually. So You are the mighty God, and the tender one, the Shepherd of Your people at the same time.

80.0.2.en: 2- When the psalmist calls upon God who sits upon the cherubim, he reminds Him that He created His people with a heavenly nature, when He created the spirit in them, that they might know Him and praise Him like the angels; therefore the psalmist asks God to shepherd His people, and lead them, and free them from their captivity, that they may glorify Him.

80.1.0.en: 2- Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh awaken thy might, and come and save us.

80.1.1.en: The psalmist calls upon the mighty, powerful God to awake; for he considered His silence over the humiliation of His people as if He were a sleeping person. So he asks Him to move and awake from His sleep, and to save His people. And he mentions these three tribes, Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, to symbolize all the people of Israel, and these three tribes used to march before the Ark of the Covenant of God when the tribes moved on their march during their stay in the wilderness of Sinai; because they are strong tribes, but now they are enslaved in captivity and weak, so the psalmist implores God to rescue His weak people and restore them to their strength, as these three tribes once were.

80.2.0.en: 3- Turn us again, O God, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved.

80.2.1.en: 1- At the end of this passage he asks God to return to the care of His people whom He neglected by disciplining them in the period of captivity, that is, return to Your care for Your people to bring us back from the captivity, so that we regain our freedom and dignity.

80.2.2.en: 2- He also asks God to cause His face to shine upon His people, so that they may receive salvation. For the appearing of God's face, or His dwelling in the midst of His people, is the life that He grants them, so that they leave the darkness of sin and live a spiritual life in Him, filled with righteousness and virtues, and this is salvation, not only from the bondage of captivity, but it is freedom and the enjoyment of fellowship with God.

80.2.3.en: 3- This verse is a refrain that is repeated in this psalm three times, in (vv. 3, 7, 19); because this is the aim of the psalm, that God bring His people back from captivity and let them enjoy His light and His salvation.

80.2.4.en: I wish this verse would be a constant petition for us; that God may bring us back from our sins into His embrace, so that we are enlightened by His light and enjoy His salvation in His Church.

80.3.0.en: 4- O LORD God of hosts, how long wilt thou smoke against the prayer of thy people?

80.3.1.en: The writer reminds God that He is the God of hosts, that is, the mighty One, able to do all things. And he asks Him, why do You smoke against the prayer of Your people? That is, why do You reject it, neglect it, and not respond, so that they remain in the humiliation of the bondage of captivity?! Is not the discipline that they have received enough, that You might forgive them and bring them back from their captivity?!

80.4.0.en: 5- Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure.

80.4.1.en: 1- The psalm describes the state of the captive people and how God allowed their food to be mixed with their tears; tears of pain, and tears of repentance.

80.4.2.en: 2- The tears that God allowed to His people were very many, so they were by measure, but at the same time they were by measure; that is, in a fixed amount that does not exceed it lest they be swallowed up by despair. And their amount may differ from one person to another according to his need for discipline and tears. And the purpose in the end is the salvation of His people.

80.5.0.en: 6- Thou makest us a strife unto our neighbours: and our enemies mock among themselves.

80.5.1.en: 1- The enemies of God's people are the nations surrounding them, that is, their neighbors, who are the Moabites and the Ammonites on the east, the Edomites in the south, and the Philistines in the west. These contended among themselves over who would take vengeance on the Jews and hand them over to the Babylonians when Nebuchadnezzar attacked them; that is, they contended and took counsel together to destroy them.

80.5.2.en: 2- This is also a prophecy about those who believe in Christ, whom their enemies mocked, namely the Jews, the Greeks and the Romans, because of the Christians' faith in a crucified person who had died; since these enemies did not know that He is God, our Redeemer.

80.6.0.en: 7- Turn us again, O God of hosts, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved.

80.6.1.en: This verse is repeated, for it is the refrain found at the end of each group of verses, and it was already explained in (v. 3). And it means here the hope of returning from captivity, and salvation from all the sufferings that God's people endured in captivity, which are mentioned in (vv. 4-6).

80.6.2.en: If you are passing through afflictions by which you suffer and your soul is crushed, trust that God has allowed them to you so that you may repent of your sins, and that your prayers may grow, and you may experience new depths in your relationship with God, and so your heart is comforted.

80.7.0.en: 8- Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it.

80.7.1.en: 1- The psalm likens God's people to a vine because it is a weak plant that needs care. And when it is cared for it gives sweet and abundant fruit. So God brought His people out of Egypt when He brought them out with a high arm from the bondage of Egypt by the ten plagues, and divided the Red Sea, and brought them across the wilderness of Sinai, and brought them to the land of Canaan, and drove out the nations living in the land, and settled them in their place. Because they were the only people who believed in God, unlike the rest of the pagan world, God therefore cared for them, led them, sustained them, and settled them in a land flowing with milk and honey.

80.7.2.en: 2- The Church is also called the vine for the same reasons as above. For the Church is the new people of God, and therefore in the hymn "O Lord, God of the Powers" we give the Church the title of the vine.

80.8.0.en: 9- Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land.

80.8.1.en: God prepared the way before His people, so He troubled the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, and they feared God who walks in the midst of His people, because they had heard of the dividing of the Red Sea, in addition to the dividing of the River Jordan. And this helped His people to be victorious over their enemies, and they dwelt in their place after they had driven them out. And they became established as the vine is established by stretching its roots in the earth, that is, its roots took root, and the roots spread in the earth and filled it; that is, the people were victorious and continued driving out the pagan peoples, and this happened in the reign of David and Solomon.

80.9.0.en: 10- The hills were covered with the shadow of it, and the boughs thereof were like the cedars of God. 11- She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river.

80.9.1.en: 1- The psalm continues its speech about the vine, and declares that it extended to cover the mountains, that is, the people settled and spread over the mountains of the land of Canaan. And it likens the people also to cedar trees, that is, the people became strong, and firm in the land, and rising up to heaven. And it declares also that it extended from the sea, meaning the Mediterranean Sea, to the river, meaning the Euphrates River, and the River of Egypt, which fills seasonally in the winter season and is found in the wilderness of Sinai.

80.9.2.en: 2- These two verses are a symbol of the spread of Christianity in the whole world across the seas and rivers, while the mountains are a symbol of rising toward heaven in the life of believers. In sum, believers in the New Testament live a heavenly life, raised above earthly things, like those who dwell on the mountains, and become strong like the cedars of Lebanon, and live by the streams of waters, that is, the work of the Holy Spirit overflows in their lives.

80.10.0.en: 12- Why hast thou then broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her? 13- The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it.

80.10.1.en: 1- The psalmist asks, and says to the Lord, why have You broken down the walls of this vine? That is, Your people, and by this he means the pulling down of the walls of Jerusalem, and burning it and its temple, and the attack of the Assyrians, then the Babylonians, and their taking possession of its good things, and after them Antiochus the king came in the days of the Maccabees, and attacked Jerusalem and Judea.

80.10.2.en: So the pig of the wood and the wild beast of the field are symbols of Assyria and Babylon, and those who pass by the way are symbols of the enemies of the Jews who lived around them, who are the pagan peoples; Moab, the sons of Ammon, Edom, and Philistia. All these gloated over the fall of Jerusalem and all the land of the Jews, and seized the Jews who were fleeing, and handed them over to Assyria and Babylon.

80.10.3.en: 2- The enemies of God's people are the demons in every generation, who gloat over the believers if they fall, and humiliate them by sin.

80.11.0.en: 14- Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine;

80.11.1.en: 1- The psalmist calls upon God and gives Him the title God of hosts. It is noticed that the expression "God of hosts" is repeated four times in this psalm; because God is the Almighty, the strong, who governs the whole world with its four corners.

80.11.2.en: 2- The psalmist asks four acts of God, which are:

80.11.3.en: a- "Return": that is, go back to Your fatherhood and Your love and Your first concern for Your people, after You had forsaken them for a time to discipline them.

80.11.4.en: b- "Look down": that is, look with care and calm, and this looking is from heaven, and means a pure spiritual look, which pours tenderness and love upon the people and raises them up to heavenly things.

80.11.5.en: c- "Behold": that is, look closely and concentrate Your care on Your people because they are weak and in need of all Your concern; it is a pleading and a hope that God will give the people all His love.

80.11.6.en: d- "Visit": that is, shepherd Your people and care for their growth, and remove everything that hinders them from You, as the sower takes care to fertilize the plant and to resist harmful pests.

80.12.0.en: 15- And the plant which thy right hand hath planted, and the son whom thou hast chosen for thyself.

80.12.1.en: 1- Here he describes God's people as a plant that God planted, which is therefore firm and strong, since God's right hand and His power are what planted His people. And he likens it also to the son, because God cares for it as a father, and He chose it from among all the peoples, and brought it out of Egypt to live to Him in the right faith.

80.12.2.en: 2- This verse is clear about the Incarnation of Christ, whom the Father planted among human beings by His Incarnation, and He is the Son of God whom He chose from among all human beings, because He alone is able to redeem us; God who became man.

80.13.0.en: 16- It is burned with fire, it is cut down: they perish at the rebuke of thy countenance.

80.13.1.en: 1- The vine that symbolizes God's people, when it turned aside to the worship of idols, God allowed it to be burned and cut down, and this was done at the hand of Nebuchadnezzar who burned the temple and Jerusalem. And so God used Nebuchadnezzar to rebuke His people and discipline them, so many died and the rest lived in bondage and humiliation; that they might return to God.

80.13.2.en: 2- By the Incarnation of Christ He rebuked evil, and destroyed sin so that it had no power over Him, and when the Jews refused to believe, the Romans rose against them in AD 70, and burned and destroyed Jerusalem and its temple.

80.14.0.en: 17- Let thy hand be upon the man of thy right hand, upon the son of man whom thou hast chosen for thyself.

80.14.1.en: This verse focuses fundamentally on the incarnate Christ, so it asks the Father that His hand be upon the man of His right hand, who is Christ, and the son of man whom the Father chose, and the hand of the Father is upon the Son, that is, the divinity works in Christ in the following:

80.14.2.en: 1- Giving Him strength, so that the Jews could not lay hold of any fault in Him, and could not seize Him before the time (Jn 8:59).

80.14.3.en: 2- Glorifying Him with miracles and mighty teachings (Jn 17:4).

80.14.5.en: 4- Sending His Holy Spirit to pour out the results of salvation and Christ's redemption upon the Church through the Sacraments, the gifts, and the fruits of the Holy Spirit.

80.15.0.en: 18- So will not we go back from thee: quicken us, and we will call upon thy name.

80.15.1.en: 1- If God takes care of His people He keeps them and establishes them in the faith, so that they do not turn back from Him, and gives them the grace of life in Him, keeping away from the death of sin, and then they glorify Him, praise Him, and thank Him for His works.

80.15.2.en: 2- This is also a prophecy about the incarnate Christ the Redeemer, who establishes believers in the faith, makes them alive from the death of sin, and raises them to eternal life, so that they glorify Him not only on earth, but also in heaven forever.

80.16.0.en: 19- Turn us again, O LORD God of hosts, cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved. This verse is the refrain repeated here for the third time, and it was already contemplated, see (v. 3). And God's shining upon us concerns eternity, where believers enjoy the luminous, exalted, perfect life.

80.16.1.en: Ask God every day to take care of your soul and shepherd it, that it may grow in His love. And seek Him in every difficult situation, then your heart will be at peace whatever difficult circumstances confront you. And do not reject His voice if He calls you to any spiritual work, whether by a voice inside you or one you hear around you.

80.16.2.en: The people's call to repentance. To the chief Musician upon Gittith. Of Asaph. "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob" (v. 1) Introduction:

80.16.3.en: 1- Its writer: Asaph, the chief of the singers in the days of David. It may be that David is the writer, and he gave it to Asaph to sing.

80.16.5.en: At the new moons, the feast of trumpets, the feast of Passover, and in the feasts in general, because it offers glorification to God.

80.16.6.en: 3- It is mentioned in the title of this psalm that it is said upon Gittith, which is a musical instrument taken from the Philistine city of Gath..

80.16.7.en: 4- The idea of the psalm is a call to God's people to repent of their disobedience, that they may regain their position as a people who believe in God, and so glorify Him.

80.16.8.en: 5- This psalm is suitable for every person to repeat at all times, to repent and regain his strong relationship with God, and so return to his strong prayers and his praises.

80.16.9.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
